query:
What is standard practice for cleaning woven-wire metal test sieves between different metal-alloy powders so that one alloy does not cross-contaminate the next? Our specific case: we just sieved a bronze (Cu-Sn) powder through a 63 um (about 230 mesh) and a 250 um (about 60 mesh) test sieve, and next we want to sieve an aluminum-alloy powder (e.g., AlSi10Mg or a new Al alloy) through the same two sieves as feedstock for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Please cover, with citations, DOIs or standard numbers:

(1) Cleaning methods for test sieves (ASTM E11 / ISO 3310-1) per standards and sieve-maker guidance (e.g., ASTM B214, ASTM E2427, ISO 2591-1, MPIF Standard 05, and sieve-maker handbooks), and how they differ between a fine 63 um mesh and a coarser 250 um mesh: dry methods (tapping, soft brushing from the underside, vacuum, low-pressure air) versus wet methods (ultrasonic bath: frequency, detergent or solvent, time, temperature), rinsing and drying (temperature limits for epoxy- or solder-bonded mesh), and what damages fine meshes (stiff or wire brushes, pushing trapped particles through with needles, high-pressure air, overloading).

(2) Whether cleaning alone is considered enough for additive-manufacturing-grade powder, or whether dedicated sieves for each alloy family are standard practice (e.g., ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52904, NASA MSFC-SPEC-3717, or industry powder-handling guidance). How do labs verify that a sieve is clean before switching alloys (backlit or stereo-microscope inspection of the mesh, weighing, wipe or tape tests, running a sacrificial flush portion of the new powder, SEM-EDS or ICP-OES of the first aluminum powder for Cu and Sn)?

(3) How much Cu-Sn particle contamination matters in aluminum LPBF powder: documented cross-contamination cases in powder bed fusion (foreign-alloy particles in Ti-6Al-4V, aluminum, nickel or steel powders), the defects they cause (inclusions, unmelted particles, Cu-rich regions, cracking, corrosion), and any quantified tolerance limits or detection thresholds.

(4) Safety: any hazard from residual bronze (possibly surface-oxidized, CuO/Cu2O) mixing with fine aluminum powder (thermite, combustible dust, NFPA 484), and how to safely clean aluminum-powder residue off the sieves afterwards (wet or ultrasonic cleaning producing hydrogen, wet aluminum fines, solvent choice, waste disposal).

(5) A step-by-step cleaning and verification procedure suitable for a small university lab, distinguishing recommendations that are well supported by the literature or standards from those that rest on vendor guidance or common practice.

Context: university materials lab making small batches of alloy powder (ultrasonic atomization) for LPBF, sieving by hand or on a sieve shaker with standard round test sieves.
task_summary: Cleaning Verification And Risk Assessment For Woven Wire Sieves Between Bronze And Aluminum Powders

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only

        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: What is standard practice for cleaning woven-wire metal test sieves between different metal-alloy powders so that one alloy does not cross-contaminate the next? Our specific case: we just sieved a bronze (Cu-Sn) powder through a 63 um (about 230 mesh) and a 250 um (about 60 mesh) test sieve, and next we want to sieve an aluminum-alloy powder (e.g., AlSi10Mg or a new Al alloy) through the same two sieves as feedstock for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Please cover, with citations, DOIs or standard numbers:

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal additive manufacturing (AM) in AlSi10Mg is enabling a new generation of lightweight and functionally optimised mirrors for aerospace, astronomy, and Earth observation. Common manufacturing routes use single point diamond turning to generate the reflective surface in the AlSi10Mg alloy leading to good reflectivity in the near infrared and visible wavelengths, further, it is often a precursor to optical polishing for shorter wavelength applications. However, the good reflectivity can be detrimentally affected by the generation of scratches on the reflective surface and this in turn limits the uptake in AM to create lightweight mirrors. Therefore, understanding the initiation of the scratch and its origin, supports improving AM mirror fabrication chains and harnessing the design benefit of AM. This study collated six AM AlSi10Mg mirrors from different projects, built using four different printers in three different production environments, and analysed the scratch initiation sites for morphology and elemental composition using scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy. The results highlighted scratches generated by aluminium oxide (Al
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ), a contaminant almost inherent in the AM process; titanium alloy (Ti6Al4V), a contaminant from printer powder exchanges; and Ti6Al4V and stainless-steel alloy (316L), contaminants from the manufacturing production environment. The results imply that to reduce scratches, AlSi10Mg only printers should be used with minimum powder recycling, further, printers should operate robust cleanliness within the manufacturing production environment to avoid cross contamination between printers.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is one of the most widely used additive manufacturing techniques for fabrication of components with complex geometries for various industrial applications including aerospace, medical and automotive. The unconsumed powder after part manufacturing is often recovered and recycled to improve process efﬁciency. How-ever, some of the particles in the recycled powder can have different physical and chemical properties from those in the virgin powder owing to their exposure to the complex environment during the manufacturing process. In addition, some contaminants can be introduced in the recycled powder due to poor process control. A number of studies have been published in the past few years revealing the effects of powder recycling on the build properties. The present work aims to highlight the key phenomena during the manufacturing process that caused degradation to the recycled powder. Further to this, some comments, gaps and areas that deserve further detailed studies are also highlighted.

Abstract:
Following observations of microcracking in two, out of three, Additive manufactured (AM) 316L steel samples, an investigation was undertaken to ascertain the root cause. Welding diagrams, taking into account composition and process parameters, could not generally account for the experimental observations of non-cracked versus cracked AM 316L samples. EBSD phase maps in all three AM samples exhibited a fully austenitic microstructure not only in the bulk sample but also near-surface. Analysis of microcracked regions in the AM samples showed the presence of local enrichment of Ni, Cu and P. Automated SEM/EDS analysis on feedstock powder samples prepared for cross-section examination revealed a fine, foreign particulate contaminant, expected to arise from NiCrCuP alloy cross-contamination during atomization, to be completely embedded in a 316L powder particle. This type of contamination would not have been revealed on examination of powder mounted onto a SEM stub, a common approach to assess powder quality. Based on this analysis, it is recommended to consider including automated SEM/EDS analysis on powder cross-sections in any standardization protocol for quality control of powders, to increase the chances of detection and identification of fine cross-contaminants. It is also recommended that atomization of NiCrCuP alloy should no longer precede atomization of 316L alloy.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND
Amidst the rapidly emerging additive manufacturing (AM) industry, not enough attention has been given to dermal exposure, with only one previous study that assessed dermal exposure to metals. Our study aimed to characterise a cobalt (Co)-chrome (Cr) alloy feedstock powder (CO-538) in terms of particle size, shape, and elemental composition, and assess dermal exposure and workplace surface contamination during powder bed fusion AM.


METHODS
Particle size distribution (PSD) and shape of the virgin and used feedstock powder were determined using static image and scanning electron microscopy analyses. The elemental composition of powders was established using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry. A removal wipe sampling method using Ghostwipes was performed on AM operators' skin at various locations (index finger, palm, wrist, back of the hand, and neck), before and after each AM processing phase. Workplace surfaces (both AM and non-AM areas) were also sampled before and after each shift using a removal wipe method to measure surface contamination.


RESULTS
PSD analysis revealed a significant difference (P ≤ 0.05) in median size, with used powder exhibiting smaller particles than virgin, where 10% of particles were smaller than the given diameter. Additionally, significant differences (P ≤ 0.05) were noted in the mean circularity and convexity between virgin and used powders, indicating that used powder particles were more irregular and rougher compared to virgin. The CO-538 feedstock powder contained Co, Cr, molybdenum (Mo), aluminium (Al), iron (Fe), and Ni. These metals were also detected on the skin of AM operators and on surfaces within the AM and non-AM areas of the facility. Dermal exposure occurred on all of the anatomical areas, with the highest total metal concentration detected on the index finger during the post-processing phase of AM. The highest full-shift geometric mean GM concentration of each metal was detected on the finger and followed a trend of Co > Cr > Fe > Al > Mo > Ni. Surface contamination occurred on all AM and non-AM sampling areas after a full shift.


CONCLUSIONS
Dermal exposure to all CO-538 alloy metal constituents occurred on all sampled anatomical areas during all three processing phases. Measurable concentrations of metals that were detected on all sampled surfaces indicate that cross-contamination between AM and non-AM areas occurs and that these surfaces may act as a secondary source of exposure. There is thus a need for control measures to be implemented in AM facilities to eliminate or reduce surface metal contamination and dermal exposure.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder bed fusion (PBF) and directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing use feedstock powders that contain metals associated with skin diseases. We performed a survey of surface contamination and limited task-based dermal exposure assessment (four employees) at a PBF and DED facility. Skin wipes of wrists for two employees in the PBF room had higher post-task levels of chromium, cobalt, molybdenum, and nickel. Personal clothing worn by PBF employees showed evidence of contamination with metals as did personal protective equipment (PPE). Microscopy analysis documented contamination of metals throughout most areas of the facility. Levels of metals on surfaces throughout the facility were (ng/cm2) <5.0–7247 (aluminum), <0.2–4899 (chromium), <background-6.0 (chromium VI), 0.03–468.1 (cobalt), 1.6–100.0 (copper), 32.9–19,000 (iron), 0.01–789.0 (molybdenum), 0.1–12,058 (nickel), 0.1–482.8 (titanium), and 0.07–9.3 (vanadium). Levels were significantly lower in administrative areas compared with the production area but generally did not differ among powder handling and non-powder handling rooms in production. The small number of participants in the dermal exposure assessment and uniqueness of the facility might limit generalizability of the results. At least for this facility, steps to lower skin contact with metals can include washing, consistent use of PPE, and increasing awareness of dermal hazards among workers. Approaches to reduce migration of metals throughout a facility can include using adhesive (“tacky”) mats and boot covers and frequent wet cleaning of floors, tools, handles, and high touch surfaces.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metal powders are key to metal additive manufacturing technologies such as powder bed fusion. These powder feedstocks experience a range of forces and physical phenomena both during the powder bed fusion process and additional post-processing stages that can alter their composition and material properties. To evaluate such effects, these powders need to be characterized, tested, and analyzed at critical stages of their lifecycles. This paper provides a review of the current state of the art for powder evaluation methods and their applicability for powder bed fusion production. Methods are categorized by the properties they evaluate, either particulate or bulk properties. Industry standards are identified for each method if applicable and the advantages and disadvantages of each are defined. Effects of these properties on the flowability and spreadability of powders are synthesized and practical management guidelines are defined. This paper aims at providing an overview of powder evaluation for powder bed fusion, practical considerations for the development of powder test and evaluation programs, and provide insights for future research undertakings in the field.

Abstract:
This work studies the tensile properties of Ti-6Al-4V samples produced by laser powder bed based Additive Manufacturing (AM), for different build orientations. The results showed high scattering of the yield and tensile strength and low fracture elongation. The subsequent fractographic investigation revealed the presence of tungsten particles on the fracture surface. Hence, its detection and impact on tensile properties of AM Ti-6Al-4V were investigated. X-ray Computed Tomography (X-ray CT) scanning indicated that these inclusions were evenly distributed throughout the samples, however the inclusions area was shown to be larger in the load-bearing plane for the vertical specimens. A microstructural study proved that the mostly spherical tungsten particles were embedded in the fully martensitic Ti-6Al-4V AM material. The particle size distribution, the flowability and the morphology of the powder feedstock were investigated and appeared to be in line with observations from other studies. X-ray CT scanning of the powder however made the high density particles visible, where various techniques, commonly used in the certification of powder feedstock, failed to detect the contaminant. As the detection of cross contamination in the powder feedstock proves to be challenging, the use of only one type of powder per AM equipment is recommended for critical applications such as Space parts.

Abstract:
This paper aims to review some important microstructural defects arising in the alloys manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) or laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). During the manufacturing process, various defects can occur in metals, which can negatively impact their mechanical properties and structural integrities. These defects include gas pores, lack of fusions, keyholes, melt pools, cracks, inclusions, and segregations. In this review, heterogeneities such as inclusion and segregation defects are discussed. Other types of defects have been comprehensively discussed in other reviews. Inclusions refer to foreign ceramic particles that are present within the metal, whereas segregations refer to the uneven distribution of alloying elements within the microstructure of the metal. The cause of appearance, effect of different parameters, and methods to reduce them in the final part are also reviewed. The effects of these defects on the integrity of the produced parts are discussed. Solutions for the elimination or minimization of these defects are also suggested. Post treatments and modifications of an alloy’s composition can also help to improve its material properties and reduce its defect concentration.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Cross-contamination during metal powder blending in multi-material laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is a common production challenge and a key barrier to the wider industrial adoption of the process. In the present investigation, the effect of different CuCr1Zr foreign-particle cross-contamination rates of up to 5.0 wt.%, simulating different cross-contamination levels in an AlSi10Mg feedstock for PBF-LB/M, is examined. The resulting metallurgical features and tensile mechanical properties of the produced components were compared to those of reference specimens manufactured from uncontaminated powder. A microstructural analysis of CuCr1Zr contaminated samples revealed characteristic Cu-rich regions, demonstrating that the higher the level of cross-contamination is, the larger these regions are. Tensile yield stress is almost linearly increased with the contamination level while the opposite trend is noticed for tensile elongation at fracture. Two different stages of strain-hardening were noticed, with Stage I exhibiting a lower strain-hardening exponent, while higher strain-hardening exponents (>0.27) were noticed for Stage II, with the latter decreasing with increasing cross-contamination level. The tensile mechanical behaviour of PBF-LB/M specimens was evaluated for the first time with appropriate quality indices, which were initially developed for similar cast aluminium alloys. Overall, the quality index accounting for global tensile performance was decreased for all build directions with increasing cross-contamination level. Despite the lower quality index at the non-contamination level, the inclined (45°) printed specimens presented quality indices that were almost unaffected by the cross-contamination level.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The article is devoted to the compressive review of the defects observed in the products of the machinery usage made mainly of anti-corrosion steels of the martensite-austenite group, difficult to process materials such as pure titanium, nickel, and their alloys, super and high entropy alloys and triple fusions produced by laser additive manufacturing, particularly the laser powder bed fusion. Abstract:
The goal of this work is to detect the onset of material cross-contamination in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process using data from in situ sensors. Material cross-contamination refers to trace foreign materials that may be introduced in the powder feedstock used in the process due to reasons such as poor cleaning of the machine after previous builds or inadequate quality control during production and storage of the powder. Material cross-contamination may lead to deleterious changes in the microstructure of the AM part and consequently affect its functional properties. Accordingly, the objective of this work is to develop and apply a spectral graph theoretic approach to detect the occurrence of material cross-contamination in real-time as the part is being built using in-process sensors. The central hypothesis is that transforming the process signals in the spectral graph domain leads to early and more accurate detection of material cross-contamination in L-PBF compared to the traditional delay-embedded Bon-Jenkins stochastic time series analysis techniques, such as autoregressive (AR) and autoregressive moving average (ARMA) modeling. To test this hypothesis, Inconel alloy 625 (UNS alloy 06625) test parts were made at Edison Welding Institute (EWI) on a custom-built L-PBF apparatus integrated with multiple sensors, including a silicon photodetector (with 300 nm to 1100 nm optical wavelength). During the process, two types of foreign contaminant materials, namely, tungsten and aluminum particulates, under varying degrees of severity were introduced. To detect cross-contamination in the part, the photodetector sensor signatures were monitored hatch-by-hatch in the form of spectral graph transform coefficients. These spectral graph coefficients are subsequently tracked on a Hotelling T2 statistical control chart. Instances of Type II statistical error, i.e., probability of failing to detect the onset of material cross-contamination, were verified against X-ray computed tomography (XCT) scans of the part to be within 5% in the case of aluminum contaminant particles. In contrast, traditional stochastic time series modeling approaches, e.g., ARMA, had corresponding Type II error exceeding 15%. Furthermore, the computation time for the spectral graph approach was found to be less than one millisecond, compared to nearly 100 ms for the traditional time series models tested.

Abstract:
The traditional methods of fighting metal fires are not always safe for firefighters. The sand and salts that are thrown onto the fire to suffocate the flames can lead to splashes of molten metal, putting the firefighters and the surroundings at risk. A novel process is described where magnesium fires are brought under control using a simple two-step process. First, coated cellulose flakes, which contain approx. 30% inorganic salts, are blown onto the fire from a distance of several meters. Due to its low bulk density, the material settles smoothly on the fire and immediately covers the flames for several seconds. Before the hot metal can break through this cover, a fine water spray is applied to the fire. The water spray wets the top layer of the cellulose flakes, which will begin to char from the bottom. The water evaporates from within the cellulose flake layer and withdraws heat. It was observed that no hydrogen is formed and that this technique can safely control fires. It is judged that 90 kg of flakes could safely bring a pile of 75 kg of burning Mg flakes under control. By using a pneumatic conveying unit for the flakes, firefighters can effectively and efficiently cover the flames from a safe distance. This novel method could be recommended to firefighters in industrial magnesium processing plants, as well as local firefighters in the vicinity of such plants.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing is now taking the lead over traditional manufacturing techniques in applications such as aerospace and biomedicine, which are characterized by low production volumes and high levels of customization. While fulfilling these requirements is the strength of metal additive manufacturing, respecting the tight tolerances typical of the mentioned applications is a harder task to accomplish. Powder bed fusion (PBF) is a class of additive manufacturing in which layers of metal powder are fused on top of each other by a high-energy beam (laser or electron beam) according to a computer-aided design (CAD) model. The quality of raw powders for PBF affects the mechanical properties of additively manufactured parts strongly, and therefore it is crucial to avoid the presence of any source of contamination, particularly cross-contamination. In this study, the identification and quantification of cross-contamination in powders of Ti-6Al-4V and maraging steel was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) techniques. Experimental results showed an overall good reliability of the developed method, opening the way for applications in machine learning environments.

From text 'mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18'.

A Mfg. Test sieving: principles and procedures. Unknown journal, 2001.

Between different metal powders, test sieves should be cleaned thoroughly so they are clean and uncontaminated before reuse, preventing carryover between samples. The excerpt recommends regular ultrasonic cleaning: immerse the sieve in mild detergent and water, then dry it thoroughly before use. For interim cleaning, gentle brushing is recommended only for mesh sizes 100 and coarser, using a nylon-bristle paintbrush with bristles approximately 25.4 mm (1 inch) long. Brush from the underside with a gentle circular motion. Vigorous brushing can distort openings, loosen the wire cloth, and reduce sieve life. Brushing should be avoided on meshes finer than 100 because their fine wires can bend, distort, or break; particles lodged in openings should instead be removed ultrasonically and never with a sharp object. Compressed-air cleaning is also cautioned against, particularly for fine meshes, because a concentrated jet can cause severe localized damage and reduce mesh accuracy. The excerpt does not mention vacuum cleaning or specify temperature limits for drying sieves, so those details cannot be established from this passage.

The sieve frame may be tapped gently to dislodge particles between brush strokes. Needles and other sharp objects must never be used because they can damage the wire cloth. Extra care is required for sieves finer than 80 mesh: brushing can distort or create irregularities in the openings, which could alter the sieve cut point. ## pqac-00000005

From text 'horn2019metalpowdercrosscontaminations pages 7-10'.

M Horn, G Schlick, M Lutter-Guenther, and C Anstaett. Metal powder cross-contaminations in multi-material laser powder bed fusion: influence of cucr1zr particles in alsi10mg feedstock on part properties. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt reports that CuCr1Zr cross-contamination in AlSi10Mg during laser powder bed fusion produces Cu-rich enclosures and primarily forms the brittle intermetallic phase Al2Cu. At low contamination, foreign phases remain isolated and act as defects that weaken the material; around 0.5 wt.% they appear as single isolated inclusions. At 3 wt.%, inclusions become more numerous and begin to interconnect, while at 5 wt.% they form larger, network-like Cu-rich regions. These transition zones and Al2Cu-rich structures exhibit predominantly brittle cleavage fracture, contributing to overall embrittlement and low ductility. Copper-rich defects can alter crack propagation and fracture direction, and their morphology may indicate microscopic hot cracking during solidification. Tensile behavior shows an initial decrease in strength at lower contamination, followed by increased yield strength and a slight tensile-strength decrease at higher contamination, when interconnected brittle phases form. The study examined 0%, 0.5%, 3%, and 5% CuCr1Zr contamination, with recycling-relevant contamination below 1 wt.% specifically discussed. The excerpt also notes that fatigue and corrosion effects were not yet established.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'horn2019metalpowdercrosscontaminations pages 1-3'.

M Horn, G Schlick, M Lutter-Guenther, and C Anstaett. Metal powder cross-contaminations in multi-material laser powder bed fusion: influence of cucr1zr particles in alsi10mg feedstock on part properties. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt directly describes a study of CuCr1Zr particles contaminating AlSi10Mg powder in laser powder bed fusion at three contamination levels: 0.5, 1.0, and 5.0 wt.% (with uncontaminated feedstock used for comparison). The contaminated AlSi10Mg microstructure contained characteristic copper-rich or “coppery” enclosures. At higher CuCr1Zr concentrations, X-ray diffraction detected Al2Cu formation. These microstructural changes were associated with overall embrittlement and reduced ultimate tensile strength. The excerpt does not explicitly report cracking or delamination caused by CuCr1Zr in the investigated samples; it presents such defects as commonly observed outcomes in foreign-particle contamination studies generally. Related literature cited in the excerpt reports that foreign particles can remain as unmelted discrete inclusions, producing lack-of-fusion defects and weakening the matrix, while other alloy contaminants may melt and form brittle intermetallic phases that cause cracking, delamination, or failure. For Al-Cu material combinations, Al2Cu formation is repeatedly linked to embrittlement. Thus, the specific CuCr1Zr evidence emphasizes copper-rich inclusions, Al2Cu formation at increased contamination, embrittlement, and decreased tensile strength, while the broader defect literature includes inclusions, cracks, delamination, and lack-of-fusion.

Increasing contamination raises the number of these structural defects, while their general shape and appearance remain broadly constant. Repeated remelting spreads copper from the enclosures into the surrounding matrix and promotes additional Al2Cu formation. Abstract:

 The utilization of additive manufacturing (AM) techniques for refractory materials in high-temperature environments has significantly expanded because of the ability to fabricate geometrically complex components. Electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-PBF), which provides lower residual stress, a cleaner vacuum environment, and better efficiency for high melting point, is one of the best-suited AM methods to produce advanced refractory components. However, the property variation attributed to the heterogeneous microstructure and process-induced defects has hindered the widespread adoption of EB-PBF-produced material like tungsten. While numerous in-situ monitoring and defect detection methods have been demonstrated for EB-PBF, a workflow that compares and evaluates process-induced abnormalities from different imaging perspectives is still limited. This study examines a feature-embedded tungsten component manufactured via the EB-PBF process to demonstrate the defect detection capabilities of a multimodal defect imaging workflow. The predefined and process-induced defects are evaluated by harnessing various imaging techniques, including in-situ electron imaging, layerwise near-infrared (NIR) imaging, post-build high-energy x-ray computed tomography (CT), and conventional destructive metallography. The results highlight the strengths and limitations of distinctive defect imaging techniques concerning specific defect types, sizes, and conditions. It was found that electron imaging can provide more abnormal detection capabilities while maintaining a higher measuring accuracy, against the conventional metallography in this case study, compared with NIR and CT imaging techniques.

Abstract:
Hydrogen, which can be produced due to the accumulation of aluminum dust that reacts with water in wet dust removal systems, is a fire and explosion hazard. To reduce hydrogen production, sodium tungstate is used in hydrogen inhibition experiments to inhibit the reaction between aluminum dust and water. The purity of the aluminum powder was 95.15%, analyzed with X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF). Each of the hydrogen inhibition experiments lasted for 12 h. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to characterize the surface morphology and composition of particles before and after the experiments. There was nearly no hydrogen produced when the concentration of the sodium tungstate solution reached 100 g/L. The results show that a protective coating containing W element was formed on the surface of the aluminum particles after the reaction with sodium tungstate, and the coating prevented the aluminum particles from contacting with water.

Abstract:
A new method is proposed to generate hydrogen in situ at low pressure from powder-pressed recycled aluminum turnings activated with small amounts of NaOH and drops of water. The contribution of this system is that the user can obtain small flows of high-purity hydrogen (>99%) to charge their portable electronic devices in remote places, in a simple, controlled, and safe way, since only water is used. Test tubes that contain tiny amounts of NaOH on their surface can be transported and used without contact. In addition to being a safer system, a smaller amount of NaOH and water is needed compared to other systems, there is no need to preheat the water, and the system can even generate heat. As the feeding is drop by drop, the hydrogen flow can be easily controlled by manual or automatic dosing. The waste obtained is solid and contains mostly aluminum hydroxide with some NaOH and impurities from the waste of origin, which are easy to sell and recycle. A study has been carried out to optimize the type of test tubes and establish critical parameters. The results show that a constant and controllable flow rate of hydrogen can be obtained depending on the drip frequency where the chemical reaction predominates over diffusion, that the optimal amount of NaOH is 20 wt%, that a finer grain size can increase the H2 yield with respect to the stoichiometric value but reduces the instantaneous flow with respect to that obtained with larger grains, and that it is very important to control the density and the impurities to increase porosity and therefore water diffusion. The estimated cost of the hydrogen produced is 3.15 EUR/kgH2 and an energy density of 1.12 kWh/kg was achieved with a test tube of 92% aluminum purity and 20 wt% NaOH.

The excerpt supports the conclusion that aluminum powder residue must not be assumed safe when exposed to water, especially if the powder is hot, burning, freshly exposed, or has damaged/rem oved oxide films. Burning or molten metals can react with water at high temperature and generate explosive hydrogen, creating a violent explosion hazard. The article specifically warns that this is a concern where wet dust collectors or water-deluge fire systems are used, and cites NFPA 484 as the applicable combustible-metals standard. For wet ultrasonic cleaning of aluminum powder residue, the excerpt therefore indicates the need for a documented combustible-metal hazard assessment, strict control of ignition and temperature, prevention of accumulated or burning dust entering the bath, ventilation and monitoring for hydrogen, and equipment designed to prevent hydrogen ignition or explosion. However, this passage does not state the specific NFPA 484 requirements, does not directly discuss aluminum–copper-oxide or aluminum–iron-oxide thermite mixtures, and does not provide detailed ultrasonic-cleaning procedures. Thermite mixtures should consequently be treated as highly energetic reactive compositions, with segregation from oxidizers and ignition sources and review of the complete NFPA 484 text and site-specific engineering controls required.

The excerpt identifies a serious fire and explosion hazard when fine aluminum powder contacts water in wet dust-collection systems: the reaction can generate hydrogen, and accumulated aluminum dust can create hazardous hydrogen concentrations. It reports that aluminum powder contacting water can produce up to 3.7–4.8 wt% hydrogen. Hydrogen is explosive in air at concentrations of approximately 4.0%–75.6% by volume, so hydrogen accumulation in enclosed equipment, ducts, tanks, or cleaning systems presents a major ignition and explosion risk. The discussion applies directly to wet scrubbers and dust removal; ultrasonic cleaning is not specifically addressed, but the same aluminum–water hydrogen-generation hazard may be relevant if fine aluminum particles are present. Precautions supported by the excerpt include preventing aluminum dust accumulation, controlling or preventing its contact with water, and managing ignition and hydrogen buildup through suitable ventilation and monitoring. The study investigated sodium tungstate as an inhibitor: at a concentration of 100 g/L, nearly no hydrogen was produced in the reported 12-hour experiments. Sodium tungstate formed a tungsten-containing protective coating on aluminum particles that blocked contact with water. Any industrial implementation should also verify inhibitor concentration, system compatibility, cleaning, and appropriate explosion-control procedures.

| Cleaning Method | Applicable Mesh Sizes | Procedure Summary | Risk of Damage to Fine Mesh | Source/Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dry tapping / inversion | **63 μm (No. 230):** yes, very gently. **250 μm (No. 60):** yes. | Invert over a labeled collector and tap the **frame**, not the cloth, gently to dislodge loose powder. Avoid impacts, cloth deflection, and attempts to force near-size particles through openings. | **Low** if tapping is gentle; hard impacts can loosen, sag, or distort the cloth. | Sieve-care guidance recommends inversion and gentle frame tapping; overloading promotes particles wedging in openings. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) |
| Soft nylon brush from underside | **63 μm (No. 230):** generally **do not brush**. **250 μm (No. 60):** acceptable. | For the 250 μm sieve, use a clean, dedicated, soft nylon paintbrush with approximately 25 mm bristles. Brush only from the underside with a light circular motion. The handbook permits brushing for **No. 100 and coarser**, meaning mesh number 100 or lower and apertures approximately 150 μm or larger. | **High at 63 μm:** brushing can bend or break wires, alter openings, and loosen cloth. **Low to moderate at 250 μm** if performed gently. | Manufacturer and NIST guidance warn that meshes finer than No. 80 to No. 100 are readily damaged by brushing or stiff bristles. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046) |
| Low-power ultrasonic bath with mild detergent | **63 μm:** preferred when compatible with the frame and bond. **250 μm:** suitable when dry cleaning is insufficient. | Immerse the sieve in a compatible mild-detergent bath and use low-power ultrasonics only long enough to release lodged particles; rinse completely and dry thoroughly. The reviewed standards and handbooks do not prescribe a universal frequency, time, or temperature. Values such as 35 to 45 kHz, 3 to 10 min, and an ambient-to-warm bath are vendor or common-practice starting points requiring manufacturer approval and validation. | **Low to moderate:** safer than brushing for fine cloth, but excessive power, time, temperature, or contact with the tank bottom can loosen bonds or fatigue mesh. | Low-power ultrasonics in mild detergent and water are preferred for delicate fine mesh; W.S. Tyler recommends mild detergent but gives no universal operating parameters. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000047) |
| Compressed air | **63 μm:** avoid. **250 μm:** only if the manufacturer permits, using clean, oil-free, low-pressure, diffuse air from a safe distance. | Never direct a concentrated jet at the cloth. If used on coarse mesh, direct diffuse airflow so particles leave the sieve rather than being driven through or embedded; contain the resulting metal-dust aerosol. | **High at 63 μm:** concentrated airflow can cause severe localized deformation and loss of aperture accuracy; it can also disperse combustible powder. | Manufacturer guidance specifically warns against compressed-air jets on fine mesh. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046) |
| HEPA vacuum | **63 μm:** possible only with noncontact, low-suction collection. **250 μm:** possible with the same precautions. | Use only a combustible-metal-rated or otherwise hazard-assessed vacuum. Keep the nozzle off the cloth, preferably collect from beneath while gently tapping the frame, and use dedicated hoses and tools for each alloy family. Do not use an ordinary shop vacuum. | **Low to moderate:** nozzle contact or high localized suction can deform fine cloth; unsuitable vacuum equipment can create ignition and cross-contamination hazards. | Common laboratory or industry practice rather than a cleaning procedure prescribed by the cited sieve standards or handbooks; combustible-metal containment and dust-cloud control require a task-specific assessment. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000040) |

Use gentle tapping or a compatible ultrasonic bath instead. | **Very high:** can enlarge or distort apertures, break wires, tear cloth, and invalidate sieve conformance. | Sieve-maker and particle-characterization guidance explicitly prohibit sharp objects and warn against stiff brushes. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046) |
| Rinsing and drying | **Both sizes; 63 μm requires especially careful handling.** | After wet cleaning, rinse until detergent and released particles are removed; allow liquid to drain without wiping the cloth. Dry completely before inspection, storage, or aluminum-powder contact. Follow the sieve maker’s bond-specific limit. One handbook states that sieve temperature must remain **below 149°C (300°F)** to prevent cloth loosening or solder-joint failure. Use a much lower validated temperature for epoxy-bonded sieves unless the manufacturer expressly approves otherwise. | **Moderate** if overheated, handled while wet, or exposed to strong thermal gradients; trapped moisture can also contaminate or oxidize powder. | Thorough drying is required. 1. Safety prep (PPE, ventilation, grounding)

4. For 63 μm sieve: no brushing - proceed to ultrasonic

7. Rinse thoroughly with deionized water

9. Visual inspection: backlit examination or stereo microscope at ~10-30x, look for trapped particles
10. Optional: tape lift test or wipe test of mesh, examine under microscope or SEM/EDS for Cu/Sn
11. Optional: sieve a small sacrificial portion of Al powder, collect, and examine by SEM/EDS or ICP for Cu/Sn
12. Document cleaning and inspection in lab notebook
13. Consider: for research-critical work, use dedicated sieves per alloy family
14. After sieving Al powder: clean immediately, consider IPA wipes rather than water; dispose of Al-contaminated waste per NFPA 484
15. Note that thermite risk from CuO+Al mixture is a documented laboratory hazard - do not store mixed residues"}

### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Step Number | Action | Details/Notes | Basis (Standard, Vendor, or Common Practice) |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prepare the work area and personnel | Review the bronze and aluminum-alloy SDSs and the laboratory combustible-metal SOP. Work in a designated, well-ventilated powder-handling area with ignition sources removed; bond or ground conductive equipment as required by the hazard assessment. Wear eye protection, suitable gloves, antistatic clothing or footwear, and respiratory protection if required. Use only a vacuum approved by the institution for the specific combustible-metal powder—never an ordinary shop vacuum. | **Safety standard/practice:** NFPA 484 principles and combustible-metal risk assessment; aluminum dust clouds, static, and unsuitable collection equipment are ignition hazards. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |
| 2 | Recover bulk bronze powder dry | Over a labeled bronze-waste or recovery container, invert the sieve and gently tap the **frame**, not the cloth. Keep Cu–Sn material segregated from aluminum feedstock and aluminum waste. Do not strike, flex, or overload the mesh. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** inversion and gentle frame tapping remove loose particles; overloading promotes wedging in openings. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) |
| 3 | Dry-clean the 250 µm sieve | Use a clean, dedicated, soft nylon brush with approximately 25 mm bristles. Brush lightly from the **underside only**, using a gentle circular motion, while collecting the released bronze. Do not force particles through the openings. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** brushing is permitted for No. 100 and coarser sieves; vigorous brushing distorts openings and loosens cloth. The 250 µm sieve is approximately No. 60. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046) |
| 4 | Do not brush the 63 µm sieve | After gentle inversion and frame tapping, take the approximately No. 230 sieve directly to compatible ultrasonic cleaning. Never use a stiff or wire brush, needle, pin, scraper, or concentrated compressed-air jet. | **Sieve-maker/NIST guidance:** brushing should be avoided on sieves finer than No. 80–100 because wires can bend, distort, or break; sharp objects and concentrated air jets can invalidate the openings. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042) |
| 5 | Remove remaining loose bronze before sonication | If wet cleaning is compatible with the sieve construction, gently rinse into a labeled Cu-containing waste vessel. Mild detergent and water are supported for bronze removal. An IPA rinse may be considered only if approved by the sieve manufacturer and laboratory flammable-solvent SOP; do **not** place a flammable solvent in an ordinary ultrasonic cleaner. | **Vendor-supported for detergent/water; conditional common practice for IPA:** solvent compatibility and an explosion-safe or indirect sonication arrangement must be established before use. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047) |
| 6 | Ultrasonically clean | Suspend the sieve so it does not rest on the ultrasonic tank bottom. Use fresh mild-detergent solution dedicated to bronze removal. A low-power bath at approximately **35–45 kHz**, ambient to about **40°C**, for **5–10 min** is a reasonable validation starting point; stop once particles are released. The cited standards and handbooks do **not** prescribe these numerical settings, so confirm them with the sieve manufacturer and validate locally. | **Supported principle:** low-power ultrasonics with mild detergent is preferred for fine cloth. **Frequency, temperature, and time:** vendor/common-practice parameters, not ASTM E11 or ISO 3310-1 requirements. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000047) |
| 7 | Rinse completely | Rinse both frame and cloth thoroughly with clean deionized water until detergent and visible particles are gone. Direct only a gentle liquid flow at the mesh; do not scrub or pressure-flush particles through it. Collect rinsate as Cu/Sn-bearing laboratory waste rather than discharging it without an approved determination. | **Sieve-care guidance plus waste practice:** forcing material through wet cloth can distort openings or tear the cloth near its joint. (pqac-00000001) |
| 8 | Dry thoroughly | Drain without wiping the cloth, then dry in clean air or a convection oven at a conservative validated temperature such as **60–80°C**. The sieve must be completely dry before contact with aluminum powder. One handbook sets an upper ceiling of **below 149°C (300°F)** to prevent loosening or solder-joint failure; this is not a recommended setpoint. Obtain the manufacturer’s lower limit for epoxy-bonded sieves. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** complete drying is required; the 149°C ceiling concerns soldered construction. The 60–80°C range is conservative common practice subject to manufacturer approval. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| 9 | Inspect mesh condition and cleanliness | Examine both faces under strong backlighting and, preferably, a stereo microscope at approximately **10–30×**. Inspect the center, perimeter, cloth-to-frame joint, underside, labels, and rolled frame seams. Reject or quarantine a sieve having trapped bronze-colored particles, blocked openings, tears, broken wires, distorted apertures, corrosion, or sagging cloth. | **Supported inspection principle; magnification is common practice:** microscopic inspection detects lodged material and cloth damage. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000046) |
| 10 | Perform a residue screen when consequence warrants | Apply a validated low-tack tape lift to the frame and peripheral joint—not in a way that pulls or deforms the fine cloth—or use a compatible wipe on the frame. Examine recovered particles optically or by SEM/EDS for Cu and Sn. A tape or wipe test is a facility-developed screening method, not a prescribed ASTM E11 or ISO 3310-1 cleanliness test. | **Common practice/analytical verification:** SEM/EDS can identify individual foreign-alloy particles that bulk chemistry or visual examination may miss. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) |
| 11 | Run a sacrificial aluminum flush | If the cleaned shared sieve must be used, pass a small, documented sacrificial portion of the new aluminum alloy through each sieve. Collect and quarantine the entire flush—do not return it to LPBF feedstock. Reinspect the sieve afterward. | **Common contamination-control practice:** sieving alone cannot guarantee removal of small foreign particles, so a flush reduces—but does not prove elimination of—carryover. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041) |
| 12 | Analyze the flush or first production fraction | For research-critical powder, sample the sacrificial flush or first aluminum fraction. Use SEM/BSE–EDS particle examination for localized Cu/Sn particles; use ICP-OES or ICP-MS for bulk Cu and Sn against an alloy-specific acceptance limit. Recognize that bulk ICP can dilute and miss rare hazardous particles, while surface-mounted SEM can miss particles embedded inside powder; polished powder cross-sections improve detection. | **Literature-supported verification:** complementary particle-scale and bulk analyses are needed because no universal detection method or cross-contamination limit exists. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000034) |
| 13 | Release or quarantine the sieve and powder | Release only if the mesh is intact, no residue is detected at the laboratory’s defined inspection level, and the flush chemistry satisfies the new alloy’s specification or project-specific limit. Otherwise repeat cleaning, replace the sieve, or reserve it permanently for Cu-base powders. Record sieve ID, prior alloy, cleaning bath, cycle settings, inspections, analytical results, and disposition. | **Quality-system/common practice:** ISO/ASTM powder-management principles emphasize documented handling, traceability, and material-specific acceptance criteria; they do not supply a universal “clean sieve” threshold. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000048) |
| 14 | Prefer dedicated sieves for consequential LPBF work | For qualification builds, new-alloy development, corrosion or fatigue studies, or any work where Cu/Sn would bias results, assign separate 63 and 250 µm sieves, pans, lids, brushes, funnels, containers, and preferably handling stations to Al alloys and Cu-base alloys. Cleaning a shared sieve is a risk-reduction measure, not proof of zero carryover. | **Strong literature/industry recommendation:** critical AM work favors one powder or alloy family per equipment set; foreign particles can evade routine certification and cause inclusions or cracking. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000060) |
| 15 | Clean safely after aluminum use and manage mixed waste | Recover aluminum residue dry under the combustible-metal SOP. Do not combine Al residue with bronze/Cu-oxide cleaning waste, and do not store mixed residues. Prefer manufacturer-approved IPA wipes for trace surface residue where the flammable-solvent SOP permits. Before aqueous or ultrasonic cleaning, remove essentially all visible Al powder and perform a hydrogen-generation assessment; water can yield H₂, especially with fine, warm, activated, or freshly exposed Al. Keep wet Al waste ventilated, unsealed, ignition-free, and dispose of it through the institution’s hazardous-waste program. Al plus CuO/Cu₂O is a potential thermite system; a laboratory Al–CuO ignition during mixing has been documented. | **Safety literature/NFPA-based practice:** aluminum is a severe combustible dust; Al–water corrosion can generate hydrogen, and Al–copper-oxide mixtures can undergo thermite reaction. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055) |

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific

Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
