artifacts.artifact-02:
| Step Number | Action | Details/Notes | Basis (Standard, Vendor, or Common Practice) |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prepare the work area and personnel | Review the bronze and aluminum-alloy SDSs and the laboratory combustible-metal SOP. Work in a designated, well-ventilated powder-handling area with ignition sources removed; bond or ground conductive equipment as required by the hazard assessment. Wear eye protection, suitable gloves, antistatic clothing or footwear, and respiratory protection if required. Use only a vacuum approved by the institution for the specific combustible-metal powder—never an ordinary shop vacuum. | **Safety standard/practice:** NFPA 484 principles and combustible-metal risk assessment; aluminum dust clouds, static, and unsuitable collection equipment are ignition hazards. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |
| 2 | Recover bulk bronze powder dry | Over a labeled bronze-waste or recovery container, invert the sieve and gently tap the **frame**, not the cloth. Keep Cu–Sn material segregated from aluminum feedstock and aluminum waste. Do not strike, flex, or overload the mesh. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** inversion and gentle frame tapping remove loose particles; overloading promotes wedging in openings. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) |
| 3 | Dry-clean the 250 µm sieve | Use a clean, dedicated, soft nylon brush with approximately 25 mm bristles. Brush lightly from the **underside only**, using a gentle circular motion, while collecting the released bronze. Do not force particles through the openings. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** brushing is permitted for No. 100 and coarser sieves; vigorous brushing distorts openings and loosens cloth. The 250 µm sieve is approximately No. 60. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046) |
| 4 | Do not brush the 63 µm sieve | After gentle inversion and frame tapping, take the approximately No. 230 sieve directly to compatible ultrasonic cleaning. Never use a stiff or wire brush, needle, pin, scraper, or concentrated compressed-air jet. | **Sieve-maker/NIST guidance:** brushing should be avoided on sieves finer than No. 80–100 because wires can bend, distort, or break; sharp objects and concentrated air jets can invalidate the openings. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042) |
| 5 | Remove remaining loose bronze before sonication | If wet cleaning is compatible with the sieve construction, gently rinse into a labeled Cu-containing waste vessel. Mild detergent and water are supported for bronze removal. An IPA rinse may be considered only if approved by the sieve manufacturer and laboratory flammable-solvent SOP; do **not** place a flammable solvent in an ordinary ultrasonic cleaner. | **Vendor-supported for detergent/water; conditional common practice for IPA:** solvent compatibility and an explosion-safe or indirect sonication arrangement must be established before use. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047) |
| 6 | Ultrasonically clean | Suspend the sieve so it does not rest on the ultrasonic tank bottom. Use fresh mild-detergent solution dedicated to bronze removal. A low-power bath at approximately **35–45 kHz**, ambient to about **40°C**, for **5–10 min** is a reasonable validation starting point; stop once particles are released. The cited standards and handbooks do **not** prescribe these numerical settings, so confirm them with the sieve manufacturer and validate locally. | **Supported principle:** low-power ultrasonics with mild detergent is preferred for fine cloth. **Frequency, temperature, and time:** vendor/common-practice parameters, not ASTM E11 or ISO 3310-1 requirements. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000047) |
| 7 | Rinse completely | Rinse both frame and cloth thoroughly with clean deionized water until detergent and visible particles are gone. Direct only a gentle liquid flow at the mesh; do not scrub or pressure-flush particles through it. Collect rinsate as Cu/Sn-bearing laboratory waste rather than discharging it without an approved determination. | **Sieve-care guidance plus waste practice:** forcing material through wet cloth can distort openings or tear the cloth near its joint. (pqac-00000001) |
| 8 | Dry thoroughly | Drain without wiping the cloth, then dry in clean air or a convection oven at a conservative validated temperature such as **60–80°C**. The sieve must be completely dry before contact with aluminum powder. One handbook sets an upper ceiling of **below 149°C (300°F)** to prevent loosening or solder-joint failure; this is not a recommended setpoint. Obtain the manufacturer’s lower limit for epoxy-bonded sieves. | **Sieve-maker guidance:** complete drying is required; the 149°C ceiling concerns soldered construction. The 60–80°C range is conservative common practice subject to manufacturer approval. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| 9 | Inspect mesh condition and cleanliness | Examine both faces under strong backlighting and, preferably, a stereo microscope at approximately **10–30×**. Inspect the center, perimeter, cloth-to-frame joint, underside, labels, and rolled frame seams. Reject or quarantine a sieve having trapped bronze-colored particles, blocked openings, tears, broken wires, distorted apertures, corrosion, or sagging cloth. | **Supported inspection principle; magnification is common practice:** microscopic inspection detects lodged material and cloth damage. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000046) |
| 10 | Perform a residue screen when consequence warrants | Apply a validated low-tack tape lift to the frame and peripheral joint—not in a way that pulls or deforms the fine cloth—or use a compatible wipe on the frame. Examine recovered particles optically or by SEM/EDS for Cu and Sn. A tape or wipe test is a facility-developed screening method, not a prescribed ASTM E11 or ISO 3310-1 cleanliness test. | **Common practice/analytical verification:** SEM/EDS can identify individual foreign-alloy particles that bulk chemistry or visual examination may miss. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) |
| 11 | Run a sacrificial aluminum flush | If the cleaned shared sieve must be used, pass a small, documented sacrificial portion of the new aluminum alloy through each sieve. Collect and quarantine the entire flush—do not return it to LPBF feedstock. Reinspect the sieve afterward. | **Common contamination-control practice:** sieving alone cannot guarantee removal of small foreign particles, so a flush reduces—but does not prove elimination of—carryover. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041) |
| 12 | Analyze the flush or first production fraction | For research-critical powder, sample the sacrificial flush or first aluminum fraction. Use SEM/BSE–EDS particle examination for localized Cu/Sn particles; use ICP-OES or ICP-MS for bulk Cu and Sn against an alloy-specific acceptance limit. Recognize that bulk ICP can dilute and miss rare hazardous particles, while surface-mounted SEM can miss particles embedded inside powder; polished powder cross-sections improve detection. | **Literature-supported verification:** complementary particle-scale and bulk analyses are needed because no universal detection method or cross-contamination limit exists. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000034) |
| 13 | Release or quarantine the sieve and powder | Release only if the mesh is intact, no residue is detected at the laboratory’s defined inspection level, and the flush chemistry satisfies the new alloy’s specification or project-specific limit. Otherwise repeat cleaning, replace the sieve, or reserve it permanently for Cu-base powders. Record sieve ID, prior alloy, cleaning bath, cycle settings, inspections, analytical results, and disposition. | **Quality-system/common practice:** ISO/ASTM powder-management principles emphasize documented handling, traceability, and material-specific acceptance criteria; they do not supply a universal “clean sieve” threshold. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000048) |
| 14 | Prefer dedicated sieves for consequential LPBF work | For qualification builds, new-alloy development, corrosion or fatigue studies, or any work where Cu/Sn would bias results, assign separate 63 and 250 µm sieves, pans, lids, brushes, funnels, containers, and preferably handling stations to Al alloys and Cu-base alloys. Cleaning a shared sieve is a risk-reduction measure, not proof of zero carryover. | **Strong literature/industry recommendation:** critical AM work favors one powder or alloy family per equipment set; foreign particles can evade routine certification and cause inclusions or cracking. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000060) |
| 15 | Clean safely after aluminum use and manage mixed waste | Recover aluminum residue dry under the combustible-metal SOP. Do not combine Al residue with bronze/Cu-oxide cleaning waste, and do not store mixed residues. Prefer manufacturer-approved IPA wipes for trace surface residue where the flammable-solvent SOP permits. Before aqueous or ultrasonic cleaning, remove essentially all visible Al powder and perform a hydrogen-generation assessment; water can yield H₂, especially with fine, warm, activated, or freshly exposed Al. Keep wet Al waste ventilated, unsealed, ignition-free, and dispose of it through the institution’s hazardous-waste program. Al plus CuO/Cu₂O is a potential thermite system; a laboratory Al–CuO ignition during mixing has been documented. | **Safety literature/NFPA-based practice:** aluminum is a severe combustible dust; Al–water corrosion can generate hydrogen, and Al–copper-oxide mixtures can undergo thermite reaction. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055) |

info.query:
What is standard practice for cleaning woven-wire metal test sieves between different metal-alloy powders so that one alloy does not cross-contaminate the next? Our specific case: we just sieved a bronze (Cu-Sn) powder through a 63 um (about 230 mesh) and a 250 um (about 60 mesh) test sieve, and next we want to sieve an aluminum-alloy powder (e.g., AlSi10Mg or a new Al alloy) through the same two sieves as feedstock for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Please cover, with citations, DOIs or standard numbers:

(1) Cleaning methods for test sieves (ASTM E11 / ISO 3310-1) per standards and sieve-maker guidance (e.g., ASTM B214, ASTM E2427, ISO 2591-1, MPIF Standard 05, and sieve-maker handbooks), and how they differ between a fine 63 um mesh and a coarser 250 um mesh: dry methods (tapping, soft brushing from the underside, vacuum, low-pressure air) versus wet methods (ultrasonic bath: frequency, detergent or solvent, time, temperature), rinsing and drying (temperature limits for epoxy- or solder-bonded mesh), and what damages fine meshes (stiff or wire brushes, pushing trapped particles through with needles, high-pressure air, overloading).

(2) Whether cleaning alone is considered enough for additive-manufacturing-grade powder, or whether dedicated sieves for each alloy family are standard practice (e.g., ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52904, NASA MSFC-SPEC-3717, or industry powder-handling guidance). How do labs verify that a sieve is clean before switching alloys (backlit or stereo-microscope inspection of the mesh, weighing, wipe or tape tests, running a sacrificial flush portion of the new powder, SEM-EDS or ICP-OES of the first aluminum powder for Cu and Sn)?

(3) How much Cu-Sn particle contamination matters in aluminum LPBF powder: documented cross-contamination cases in powder bed fusion (foreign-alloy particles in Ti-6Al-4V, aluminum, nickel or steel powders), the defects they cause (inclusions, unmelted particles, Cu-rich regions, cracking, corrosion), and any quantified tolerance limits or detection thresholds.

(4) Safety: any hazard from residual bronze (possibly surface-oxidized, CuO/Cu2O) mixing with fine aluminum powder (thermite, combustible dust, NFPA 484), and how to safely clean aluminum-powder residue off the sieves afterwards (wet or ultrasonic cleaning producing hydrogen, wet aluminum fines, solvent choice, waste disposal).

(5) A step-by-step cleaning and verification procedure suitable for a small university lab, distinguishing recommendations that are well supported by the literature or standards from those that rest on vendor guidance or common practice.

Context: university materials lab making small batches of alloy powder (ultrasonic atomization) for LPBF, sieving by hand or on a sieve shaker with standard round test sieves.
